h1: Peanut in food labels: how to spot it and what it's hiding.
metaTitle: Peanut allergy food guide: hidden names on labels — Nouri
metaDescription: Peanut hides under dozens of names on food labels. Nouri scans any label and flags Peanut in seconds — no ingredient-list squinting required. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Peanut allergy is one of the most prevalent food allergies in the United States and is triggered by proteins found in the peanut plant, primarily Ara h 1, Ara h 2, and Ara h 3. Even trace amounts of peanut protein can trigger a reaction in sensitive individuals, ranging from mild symptoms to anaphylaxis. Peanut is classified as one of the Big Nine major food allergens under the Food Allergy Safety, Treatment, Education, and Research (FASTER) Act, which requires mandatory label disclosure in the United States.

Under the Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act (FALCPA) and the FASTER Act, any food containing peanut as an ingredient must declare it clearly on the label — either within the ingredient list ("peanut," "peanut oil," "peanut flour") or in a separate "Contains: Peanut" statement immediately following the ingredient list. Hidden forms include: groundnuts, mixed nuts, peanut butter, peanut flour, peanut oil, peanut protein, beer nuts, earth nuts, mandelonas (peanuts reshaped to resemble tree nuts), and arachis oil. "May contain peanuts" and "manufactured in a facility that processes peanuts" are voluntary cross-contamination statements — they are not required by FALCPA but indicate a shared-production risk.

Foods most likely to contain peanut: peanut butter, candy, baked goods, granola bars, sauces (satay, mole, chili), flavored crackers, trail mix, breakfast cereals, protein bars, egg rolls.

Cross-contamination disclosures are voluntary in the US, which means their absence does not guarantee a peanut-free production environment. Nouri reads both the declared ingredient list and the advisory statements on the label, flagging all peanut-related terms against your allergen profile. h1: Gluten in food labels: how to spot it and what it's hiding.
metaTitle: Gluten allergy food guide: hidden names on labels — Nouri
metaDescription: Gluten hides under dozens of names on food labels. Nouri scans any label and flags Gluten in seconds — no ingredient-list squinting required. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Gluten is a family of proteins — primarily gliadin and glutenin — found in wheat, rye, barley, and their hybrids. In people with celiac disease, consuming gluten triggers an immune response that damages the small intestine lining. In people with non-celiac gluten sensitivity, gluten consumption causes gastrointestinal and systemic symptoms without the autoimmune intestinal damage seen in celiac. Gluten is also excluded from several dietary protocols including the Autoimmune Protocol (AIP) and some FODMAP frameworks.

Wheat is a major allergen under FALCPA and must be declared on US food labels. However, rye and barley are NOT covered by FALCPA — they do not appear in "Contains" statements unless a manufacturer adds them voluntarily, which means barley malt, barley flour, and rye flour require manual ingredient-list reading. Hidden gluten sources include: malt (typically from barley), malt vinegar, malt flavoring, brewer's yeast, wheat starch, spelt, kamut, farro, durum, semolina, triticale, and "natural flavors" derived from gluten-containing grains. Oats are naturally gluten-free but are frequently cross-contaminated; only certified gluten-free oats are considered safe for celiac.

Foods most likely to contain gluten: bread and baked goods, pasta, crackers, beer, soy sauce, seasoned chips, soups with thickeners, processed meats, grain-based cereals, sauces with malt vinegar.

The gap between wheat disclosure (required) and barley/rye disclosure (voluntary) is one of the most common label-reading failure points for people managing celiac or gluten sensitivity. h1: Milk in food labels: how to spot it and what it's hiding.
metaTitle: Milk allergy food guide: hidden names on labels — Nouri
metaDescription: Milk hides under dozens of names on food labels. Nouri scans any label and flags Milk in seconds — no ingredient-list squinting required. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Milk allergy is triggered by proteins in cow's milk, primarily casein and whey. It is distinct from lactose intolerance — lactose intolerance is a digestive issue caused by insufficient lactase enzyme, while milk allergy is an immune-mediated response to milk proteins. Milk allergy is most common in infants and young children but can persist into adulthood. Milk is one of the Big Nine major food allergens under the FASTER Act and requires mandatory label disclosure in the United States.

Under FALCPA, milk must be declared clearly on food labels in the ingredient list or in a "Contains: Milk" statement. Hidden forms of milk on labels include: butter, butter fat, butter oil, buttermilk, casein, caseinates (calcium, sodium, potassium caseinate), cheese, cottage cheese, cream, curds, ghee, half-and-half, hydrolysates (casein hydrolysate, milk protein hydrolysate, whey hydrolysate), lactalbumin, lactalbumin phosphate, lactoferrin, lactoglobulin, lactose, lactulose, milk solids, nougat, Recaldent, rennet casein, sour cream, sour cream solids, whey, yogurt. Kosher dairy labels that say "D" or "DE" also indicate milk-derived ingredients or shared equipment.

Foods most likely to contain milk: dairy products, baked goods, chocolate, protein bars, instant mashed potatoes, seasoned chips, salad dressings, margarine, non-dairy creamers (often contain sodium caseinate), canned tuna (some brands).

The sheer number of milk-derived ingredient names — over 20 common aliases — makes manual label reading error-prone, especially for the casein derivatives and hydrolysate terms that do not obviously reference dairy. h1: Soy in food labels: how to spot it and what it's hiding.
metaTitle: Soy allergy food guide: hidden names on labels — Nouri
metaDescription: Soy hides under dozens of names on food labels. Nouri scans any label and flags Soy in seconds — no ingredient-list squinting required. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Soy allergy is triggered by proteins in soybeans. It is one of the most common food allergies in children and is also frequently managed in adulthood. Soy is classified as one of the Big Nine major food allergens under the FASTER Act and requires mandatory label disclosure in the United States. Soy is also excluded from AIP, some paleo frameworks, and protocols targeting autoimmune or inflammatory conditions, making it relevant far beyond allergy contexts.

Under FALCPA, soy must be declared in the ingredient list or in a "Contains: Soy" statement. Soy hides under a wide range of names on food labels: edamame, kinako, miso, natto, shoyu, soy sauce, tamari, tempeh, tofu, bean curd, soy protein isolate, textured soy protein (TSP), textured vegetable protein (TVP), hydrolyzed soy protein, soybean oil, lecithin (often soy-derived unless labeled otherwise), soy flour, soy fiber, soy milk, soy nut, and yuba. Highly refined soybean oil and soy lecithin are exempt from the FALCPA allergen labeling requirement under a "highly refined" exception, though many soy-allergic individuals still avoid them.

Foods most likely to contain soy: tofu, tempeh, edamame, soy sauce, miso, protein bars, meat substitutes, canned soups, baked goods, cereals, infant formula, margarine, chocolate.

The exemption for highly refined soybean oil and lecithin means a product can contain soy-derived ingredients without triggering a "Contains: Soy" statement. h1: Egg in food labels: how to spot it and what it's hiding.
metaTitle: Egg allergy food guide: hidden names on labels — Nouri
metaDescription: Egg hides under dozens of names on food labels. Nouri scans any label and flags Egg in seconds — no ingredient-list squinting required. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Egg allergy is triggered by proteins found in egg white and, less commonly, egg yolk. The primary allergenic proteins are ovomucoid, ovalbumin, ovotransferrin, and lysozyme. Egg allergy is among the most common food allergies in children and can persist into adulthood. Egg is one of the Big Nine major food allergens under the FASTER Act and requires mandatory label disclosure in the United States. Egg is also excluded from vegan diets and from the Autoimmune Protocol (AIP), making it relevant across allergy and dietary-protocol contexts.

Under FALCPA, egg must be declared in the ingredient list or in a "Contains: Egg" statement. Hidden forms on labels include: albumin (also spelled albumen), apovitellin, dried egg, egg solids, egg white, egg yolk, eggnog, globulin, livetin, lysozyme, mayonnaise, meringue, meringue powder, ovalbumin, ovoglobulin, ovomucin, ovomucoid, ovotransferrin, ovovitellin, powdered egg, silici albuminate, simplesse, surimi (some formulations), trailblazer, vitellin. The term "natural flavors" occasionally masks egg derivatives, though this is uncommon.

Foods most likely to contain egg: baked goods, pasta, mayonnaise, salad dressings, quiche, custard, meatballs and meatloaf, breaded meats, waffles, some breakfast cereals, marshmallows, some wines (egg used as fining agent).

Wine and some vinegars use egg as a processing aid — these may not appear in the ingredient list because processing aids are not always required to be declared. h1: Wheat in food labels: how to spot it and what it's hiding.
metaTitle: Wheat allergy food guide: hidden names on labels — Nouri
metaDescription: Wheat hides under dozens of names on food labels. Nouri scans any label and flags Wheat in seconds — no ingredient-list squinting required. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Wheat allergy is an immune response to one or more proteins in wheat, including gluten, albumin, globulin, and gliadin. It is distinct from celiac disease and non-celiac gluten sensitivity: wheat allergy can occur with or without a gluten-mediated mechanism, and some individuals are allergic to specific non-gluten wheat proteins. Wheat is one of the Big Nine major food allergens under the FASTER Act and requires mandatory label disclosure in the United States. Unlike gluten avoidance, which also requires eliminating rye and barley, wheat-specific allergy management focuses on wheat-derived ingredients while other gluten-containing grains may or may not be relevant.

Under FALCPA, wheat must be declared in the ingredient list or in a "Contains: Wheat" statement. Hidden wheat sources include: wheat flour, whole wheat flour, bread flour, durum flour, durum wheat, semolina, spelt, kamut, farro, einkorn, emmer, bulgur, wheat bran, wheat germ, wheat starch, wheat berries, cracker meal, farro, fu (wheat gluten), seitan, triticale, hydrolyzed wheat protein, wheat-based modified food starch, and malt flavoring derived from wheat. "Modified food starch" in the US is required to declare wheat if it is wheat-derived.

Foods most likely to contain wheat: bread and baked goods, pasta, crackers, cereal, flour tortillas, soy sauce (most are wheat-containing), beer, processed soups and gravies, breaded meats, couscous, bulgur dishes.

Wheat's widespread use as a binder, thickener, and fermentation substrate means it appears in product categories — soy sauce, seasoning blends, soups — where it is not always intuitively expected. h1: Tree Nut in food labels: how to spot it and what it's hiding.
metaTitle: Tree Nut allergy food guide: hidden names on labels — Nouri
metaDescription: Tree Nut hides under dozens of names on food labels. Nouri scans any label and flags Tree Nut in seconds — no ingredient-list squinting required. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Tree nut allergy encompasses allergic reactions to a broad category of nuts that grow on trees, as distinct from peanuts which are legumes. The category includes almonds, cashews, walnuts, pecans, pistachios, macadamia nuts, hazelnuts, Brazil nuts, pine nuts, chestnuts, and coconut (though coconut's regulatory status as a tree nut is debated). Each individual tree nut has its own set of allergenic proteins, and tree nut-allergic individuals may react to one, several, or all tree nuts depending on their specific sensitization. Tree nut is classified as one of the Big Nine major food allergens under the FASTER Act and requires mandatory label disclosure.

Under FALCPA, tree nut must be declared in the ingredient list or in a "Contains: Tree Nuts" statement, with the specific nut identified where possible. Hidden forms on labels include: almond meal, almond paste, almond milk, cashew butter, walnut oil, pecan meal, praline (typically pecan or almond-based), gianduja (hazelnut-chocolate blend), marzipan (almond paste), nougat (may contain almonds or hazelnuts), nut extracts, and natural nut flavorings. Cross-reactive sensitization between tree nuts is common but not universal — an allergy to one tree nut does not automatically mean allergy to all.

Foods most likely to contain tree nuts: mixed nuts and trail mix, pesto (pine nuts), pralines and confections, nut butters, marzipan and almond paste, granola bars, baked goods, certain chocolate products, some Asian sauces, flavored coffee creamers.

Marzipan, gianduja, and praline are examples of nut-containing ingredients that may not be immediately recognizable as tree-nut sources by name alone. Nouri reads the full ingredient list and flags both direct and derivative tree-nut terms against your allergen profile. Nouri scans for Tree Nut automatically — free on iOS.

h1: Shellfish in food labels: how to spot it and what it's hiding.
metaTitle: Shellfish allergy food guide: hidden names on labels — Nouri
metaDescription: Shellfish hides under dozens of names on food labels. Nouri scans any label and flags Shellfish in seconds — no ingredient-list squinting required. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Shellfish allergy is triggered by proteins — particularly tropomyosin — found in crustacean shellfish such as shrimp, crab, lobster, crayfish, prawn, and krill. Mollusks (clams, oysters, scallops, squid, abalone) are a separate category under FALCPA and are not covered by the crustacean shellfish allergen declaration requirement — a distinction that creates a labeling gap for people managing broad seafood allergies. Crustacean shellfish allergy is one of the most common food allergies in adults and is among the top causes of severe allergic reactions requiring emergency care. Crustacean shellfish is one of the Big Nine major food allergens under the FASTER Act.

Under FALCPA, crustacean shellfish must be declared in the ingredient list or in a "Contains: Crustacean Shellfish" statement, with the specific type identified where possible. Hidden sources include: shrimp paste, shrimp extract, krill oil, crab extract, lobster stock, seafood flavoring, bouillabaisse (a classic French seafood stew), some Worcestershire sauces (some contain anchovies or shellfish derivatives), glucosamine (frequently derived from shrimp shells), and seafood flavorings in seasoning blends. Mollusks — clams, oysters, squid, scallops — are not covered by FALCPA and must be tracked by reading the ingredient text manually.

Foods most likely to contain shellfish: sushi and Asian seafood dishes, seafood soups and bisques, paella, jambalaya, Caesar dressings (some contain anchovy), glucosamine supplements, some Worcestershire sauces, bouillabaisse, seafood-flavored chips or snacks.

The FALCPA gap for mollusks — combined with shellfish concealed in flavoring compounds and supplements — means standard "Contains" statement monitoring alone is insufficient. Nouri reads the full ingredient list and flags both crustacean shellfish and common mollusk derivatives against your allergen profile. Nouri scans for Shellfish automatically — free on iOS.
